issues.legal_issue: A pre-emptor’s qualification is assessed through the decree of the court of first instance, and a subsequent loss of qualification or prospective change in law during an appeal does not defeat the decree.
material_facts: The plaintiffs claimed a preferential right to purchase as co-sharers and obtained a decree for pre-emption from the trial court.
After the decree, they deposited the purchase money as required by Order XX Rule 14 of the Code of Civil Procedure.
The decree was affirmed by the appellate courts, and a statutory amendment removing a co-sharer’s right of pre-emption came into force while a further appeal was pending.
issues.conclusion: The appellate court had to decide the appeal by reference to the parties’ substantive rights when the pre-emption suit was adjudicated; the later amendment did not affect the decree or the plaintiffs’ claim. A pre-emptor must possess the right on the date of sale, the date of filing suit, and the date of the trial court’s decree, but a loss of that right after the decree does not defeat the claim.
issues.legal_principle: The rule in Hans Nath v. Ragho Prasad Singh, Bhagwan Das v. Chet Ram, Rikhi Ram v. Ram Kumar and Didar Singh v. Ishar Singh is that the pre-emptor must retain the qualification through the trial court’s decree, not thereafter. Under Order XX Rule 14 CPC, deposit of the purchase money following a decree transfers title to the pre-emptor. The appellate court considers whether the trial court’s decree was correct on the rights then existing; subsequent events cannot displace a vested right unless a retrospective law requires that result. The Court approved Didar Singh and held that Ramjilal v. Ghisa Ram did not state the correct law.

rule.if: preemption_suit and appeal_from_preemption_decree and preemptor_qualified_through_trial_decree and trial_court_decreed_preemption and purchase_money_deposited and post_decree_qualification_loss_or_prospective_law_change

predicates.preemption_suit: A claimant brought a proceeding seeking to purchase property in preference to a buyer.
predicates.appeal_from_preemption_decree: A party appealed from a trial court’s decree in the pre-emption proceeding.
predicates.preemptor_qualified_through_trial_decree: The claimant possessed the required preferential qualification on the sale date, when suit was filed, and when the trial court adjudicated the suit.
predicates.trial_court_decreed_preemption: The trial court granted the claimant a decree for pre-emption.
predicates.purchase_money_deposited: The claimant deposited the purchase money following the decree.
predicates.post_decree_qualification_loss_or_prospe: After the trial court’s decree, the claimant lost the qualification or a prospective change in law removed the claimed right while an appeal was pending.

issues.definition: When a qualified claimant has obtained a pre-emption decree and deposited the purchase money, a later loss of qualification or prospective legal change does not prevent the decree from remaining effective.

issues.legal_issue: An amendment affecting a substantive pre-emption right does not apply retrospectively to a pending appeal unless retrospective operation is expressed or necessarily intended.
material_facts: The statutory amendment substituted a provision limiting the right of pre-emption to tenants and thereby removed a co-sharer’s basis for claiming pre-emption.
The amendment took effect after the trial court had decreed the plaintiffs’ suit and while an appeal was pending.
The substituted provision contained no express language or necessary implication making it retrospective.
issues.conclusion: The substituted provision operated prospectively and did not affect the substantive rights fixed when the trial court passed its decree; the appellate court was not required to apply it to the pending appeal.
issues.legal_principle: Substantive legislation is presumed prospective unless retrospective operation is expressly stated or follows by necessary intendment. Garikapati Veeraya v. N. Subbiah Choudhry, Dayawati v. Inderjit, Hitendra Vishnu Thakur v. State of Maharashtra, K.S. Paripoornan v. State of Kerala, and Moti Ram v. Suraj Bhan support that rule. Lachmeshwar Prasad Shukul v. Keshwar Lal Chaudhuri concerns legislation made retrospective and does not require an appellate court to apply a prospective amendment. Shantidevi v. Hukum Chand had already treated the substituted provision as prospective.

predicates.pending_preemption_appeal: An appeal in a pre-emption proceeding remained undecided when a new law came into force.
predicates.amendment_changes_substantive_right: The new law altered who could claim the substantive right to pre-emption.
predicates.no_express_or_necessary_retroactive_inte: The new law did not expressly or by necessary implication apply to rights already fixed in pending litigation.

issues.definition: A change to a substantive right applies prospectively when an appeal is pending and the new law does not indicate that it governs previously fixed rights.

issues.legal_issue: The characterization of an amendment as beneficial does not, by itself, justify construing a clear and unambiguous substantive provision as retrospective.
material_facts: The appellants argued that removing the co-sharer’s pre-emption right benefited the public generally and therefore the amendment should operate retrospectively.
The substituted provision used plain and unambiguous language and did not state that it applied retrospectively.
issues.conclusion: The Court rejected the argument that benevolent construction made the amendment retrospective; doing so would require adding words to the enactment and altering its meaning.
issues.legal_principle: Benevolent construction may assist where statutory language is ambiguous, but it cannot be used to rewrite a plain provision or create an unstated retrospective effect. Moti Ram v. Suraj Bhan establishes that a measure’s beneficial character does not determine retrospectivity. Rafiquennessa v. Lal Bahadur Chetri was distinguishable because the statutory provisions there indicated an intention to protect earlier transactions; H. Shiva Rao v. Celelia Pereira concerned ambiguous expressions.

rule.if: pending_preemption_appeal and amendment_is_claimed_to_be_beneficial and provision_is_plain_and_unambiguous and no_retroactive_intent

predicates.pending_preemption_appeal: An appeal in a pre-emption proceeding remained undecided when a new law came into force.
predicates.amendment_is_claimed_to_be_beneficial: A party argued that the amendment was enacted for the general benefit of the public.
predicates.provision_is_plain_and_unambiguous: The new provision’s words have a clear meaning and do not give rise to competing interpretations.
predicates.no_retroactive_intent: The new provision does not express or necessarily imply that it applies to earlier rights or proceedings.

issues.definition: A party’s claim that a clear amendment is beneficial does not make it retrospective when the amendment contains no indication of retroactive operation.

issues.legal_issue: A substituted provision is not declaratory or retrospective merely because it replaces an earlier provision.
material_facts: The amendment replaced the earlier provision governing pre-emption with a provision limiting the right to tenants.
The earlier provision was plain and its meaning was not in doubt; the amendment did not purport to explain an omission or clarify the meaning of the earlier provision.
The amendment contained no express or implied indication that it was intended to operate retrospectively.
issues.conclusion: The amendment was not declaratory and had no retrospective operation.
issues.legal_principle: A declaratory or explanatory enactment generally operates retrospectively when it removes an existing doubt or supplies an obvious omission in earlier law; its substance, not its label, determines its character. Keshavlal Jethalal Shah v. Mohanlal Bhagwandas and R. Rajagopal Reddy v. Padmini Chandrasekharan state this principle. Mithilesh Kumari v. Prem Behari Khare was overruled on the relevant point by R. Rajagopal Reddy. A substituted provision is subject to the ordinary rules governing amending enactments.

rule.if: preemption_law_amended_during_appeal and earlier_provision_was_clear and amendment_does_not_clarify_doubt_or_supply_omission and no_retroactive_intent

predicates.preemption_law_amended_during_appeal: A new provision governing pre-emption came into force while an appeal in a pre-emption proceeding was pending.
predicates.earlier_provision_was_clear: The prior provision had a plain meaning that was not in doubt.
predicates.amendment_does_not_clarify_doubt_or_supp: The amendment does not explain an uncertain earlier provision or fill an obvious gap in it.
predicates.no_retroactive_intent: The amendment does not expressly or by necessary implication apply to earlier rights or proceedings.

issues.definition: Replacing a clear provision without resolving a doubt or supplying an omission does not make an amendment declaratory or retrospective when retroactive intent is absent.
